\begin{frame}{Today's question and route}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question}: a stationary series is correlated with its own past; which small model captures this memory and turns it into forecasts with honest uncertainty?
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the answer of Box and Jenkins: \textbf{ARMA($p,q$)} models, a few parameters instead of infinitely many Wold weights
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Route} of the chapter
    \begin{itemize}
        \item AR($p$) and MA($q$): stationarity, invertibility, characteristic roots, ACF and PACF
        \item ARMA($p,q$): the causal MA($\infty$) form, the impulse responses, identification
        \item estimation (Yule--Walker, conditional least squares, maximum likelihood), AIC and BIC, residual diagnostics
        \item forecasting and the Box--Jenkins method on Romanian GDP, inflation, BET, EUR/RON and the sunspots
    \end{itemize}
    \item Seminar 2 comes before this lecture: it gives the formulas; here we derive them and use them on data
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Learning outcomes}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Check the stationarity of an AR($p$) and the invertibility of an MA($q$) from the roots of their polynomials
    \item Derive the mean, the autocovariances and the $\psi$ weights of AR(1), AR(2), MA($q$) and ARMA(1,1)
    \item Propose candidate orders from the ACF and the PACF, and choose among them with AIC and BIC
    \item Estimate ARMA models by Yule--Walker, conditional least squares and maximum likelihood, and read the output
    \item Test the residuals: Ljung--Box with $m - p - q$ degrees of freedom, Jarque--Bera
    \item Compute ARMA forecasts and their intervals, and explain mean reversion
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

%=============================================================================
\section{From Chapter 1 to ARMA models}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{Tools from \tsachlinkt{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter1_stochastic_processes_stationarity.pdf}{Chapter 1}}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Weak stationarity}: constant mean $\mu$ and autocovariance $\gamma(h) = \mathrm{Cov}(X_t, X_{t+h})$ that depends only on the lag $h$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item ACF $\rho(h) = \gamma(h)/\gamma(0)$; PACF $\phi_{hh}$ = correlation of $X_t$ and $X_{t+h}$ after removing $X_{t+1}, \dots, X_{t+h-1}$
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{White noise} $\varepsilon_t \sim \mathrm{WN}(0, \sigma^2)$: mean 0, variance $\sigma^2$, no autocorrelation
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the \textbf{lag operator}: $LX_t = X_{t-1}$, $L^kX_t = X_{t-k}$; polynomials in $L$ act on series
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Wold decomposition} (\refWold): every stationary, purely nondeterministic process is $X_t = \mu + \sum_{j \ge 0}\psi_j\varepsilon_{t-j}$, $\psi_0 = 1$, $\sum_j\psi_j^2 < \infty$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item details and charts: \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter1_stochastic_processes_stationarity.pdf}{Chapter 1}, sections on the lag operator, Wold and the sample ACF and PACF
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The problem: infinitely many weights}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Wold says \textbf{what} a stationary process looks like, not \textbf{how to estimate it}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\psi_1, \psi_2, \dots$: infinitely many unknowns, and only $T$ observations
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Idea}: write $\psi(L) = \sum_j\psi_jL^j$ as a \textbf{ratio of two short polynomials}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\psi(L) = \theta(L)/\phi(L)$ with $\phi(L) = 1 - \phi_1L - \dots - \phi_pL^p$, $\theta(L) = 1 + \theta_1L + \dots + \theta_qL^q$
        \item then $\phi(L)(X_t - \mu) = \theta(L)\varepsilon_t$: the \textbf{ARMA($p,q$)} model with $p + q + 2$ parameters ($\phi$, $\theta$, $\mu$, $\sigma^2$)
    \end{itemize}
    \item A rational function approximates almost any smooth $\psi(L)$ well with small $p$ and $q$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the principle of \textbf{parsimony}: the smallest model that leaves white-noise residuals
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Three building blocks}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{AR($p$)}, autoregressive: today depends on the last $p$ values of the series
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $X_t = c + \phi_1X_{t-1} + \dots + \phi_pX_{t-p} + \varepsilon_t$; origin: \refYule, sunspots
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{MA($q$)}, moving average: today depends on the last $q$ shocks
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $X_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t + \theta_1\varepsilon_{t-1} + \dots + \theta_q\varepsilon_{t-q}$; origin: \refSlutzky, sums of random causes
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{ARMA($p,q$)}: both parts; popularised as a complete method by \refBJ{} (first edition 1970)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $c$ is the \textbf{intercept}; the mean is $\mu = c/(1 - \phi_1 - \dots - \phi_p)$, not $c$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Throughout: $\varepsilon_t \sim \mathrm{WN}(0, \sigma^2)$, and for likelihood and intervals $\varepsilon_t$ i.i.d. $N(0, \sigma^2)$ (independent and identically distributed)
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{Autoregressive models}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{The AR(1) model}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $X_t = c + \phi X_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$, or $(1 - \phi L)X_t = c + \varepsilon_t$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\phi$: the share of today's deviation from the mean that survives until tomorrow
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Back substitution} $k$ times:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $X_t = c(1 + \phi + \dots + \phi^{k-1}) + \phi^kX_{t-k} + \sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\phi^j\varepsilon_{t-j}$
        \item if $|\phi| < 1$: $\phi^k \to 0$ and $X_t = \dfrac{c}{1 - \phi} + \sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\phi^j\varepsilon_{t-j}$
    \end{itemize}
    \item This is the Wold form with $\psi_j = \phi^j$: the \textbf{causal} (MA($\infty$)) representation
    \begin{itemize}
        \item causal = $X_t$ depends only on present and past shocks
        \item $\phi = 1$: random walk (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter1_stochastic_processes_stationarity.pdf}{Chapter 1}), no stationary solution; $|\phi| > 1$: explosive, or a solution that depends on future shocks, excluded
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Moments of a stationary AR(1)}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Mean}: take expectations, $\mu = c + \phi\mu$, so $\mu = c/(1 - \phi)$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item stationarity is used here: $E[X_t] = E[X_{t-1}]$
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Variance}: $\gamma(0) = \phi^2\gamma(0) + \sigma^2$, since $\varepsilon_t$ is uncorrelated with $X_{t-1}$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\gamma(0) = \sigma^2/(1 - \phi^2)$: grows without bound as $|\phi| \to 1$
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Autocovariances}: multiply $X_t - \mu = \phi(X_{t-1} - \mu) + \varepsilon_t$ by $X_{t-h} - \mu$, $h \ge 1$, and take expectations
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\gamma(h) = \phi\gamma(h - 1)$, so $\gamma(h) = \phi^h\gamma(0)$ and $\rho(h) = \phi^h$
        \item geometric decay; alternating signs if $\phi < 0$
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Half-life} of a shock: the $h$ with $\phi^h = 1/2$, i.e. $h = \ln 0.5/\ln\phi$
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Worked example: an AR(1)}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $X_t = 2 + 0.8X_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$, $\sigma^2 = 1$
    \item Stationary? $|\phi| = 0.8 < 1$: yes
    \begin{itemize}
        \item mean $\mu = 2/(1 - 0.8) = 10$; the intercept is 2, the mean is 10
    \end{itemize}
    \item Variance and ACF
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\gamma(0) = 1/(1 - 0.64) = 2.78$
        \item $\rho(3) = 0.8^3 = 0.512$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Half-life $= \ln 0.5/\ln 0.8 = 3.11$ periods
    \begin{itemize}
        \item after about 3 periods, half of a shock is gone
    \end{itemize}
    \item $\psi$ weights: $1, 0.8, 0.64, 0.512, \dots$: a shock of 1 today moves $X_{t+2}$ by $0.64$
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{AR(1) for three values of $\phi$}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch2_ar1.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}

\quantlet{TSA\_ch2\_ar\_models}{\qlurl{TSA_ch2_ar_models}}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the AR(1) paths}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\phi = 0.9$: long swings away from 0; sample $\hat\rho(1) = 0.88$, variance 4.98 (theory 5.26)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item strong persistence looks like a trend over short windows
    \end{itemize}
    \item $\phi = 0.3$: close to white noise; only $\hat\rho(1) = 0.35$ is clearly outside the band
    \begin{itemize}
        \item variance 1.18 (theory 1.10)
    \end{itemize}
    \item $\phi = -0.7$: zig-zag; $\hat\rho(1) = \ensuremath{-}0.58$, $\hat\rho(2) = 0.34$, alternating signs
    \begin{itemize}
        \item in economics: overshooting and correction, or a measurement error that is corrected next period
    \end{itemize}
    \item With $T = 200$ the sample ACF is below the theoretical one at long lags: a small-sample bias that also affects the estimators (Section 5)
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The AR($p$) model and its characteristic polynomial}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\phi(L)X_t = c + \varepsilon_t$, with $\phi(z) = 1 - \phi_1z - \dots - \phi_pz^p$, a polynomial in a complex number $z$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item factorise: $\phi(z) = (1 - \lambda_1z)\cdots(1 - \lambda_pz)$, where $z_i = 1/\lambda_i$ are the roots
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Stationarity (causality) condition}: all roots of $\phi(z) = 0$ lie \textbf{outside the unit circle}, $|z_i| > 1$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item equivalently: all \textbf{inverse roots} $\lambda_i$ lie inside, $|\lambda_i| < 1$ (the form shown by software)
        \item reason: $1/(1 - \lambda L) = \sum_j\lambda^jL^j$ converges only if $|\lambda| < 1$; each factor is an AR(1)
    \end{itemize}
    \item A root on the circle ($|z| = 1$, e.g. $z = 1$) is a \textbf{unit root}: non-stationarity, the topic of \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter3_unit_roots_arima_models.pdf}{Chapter 3}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item quick necessary check: $\phi_1 + \dots + \phi_p < 1$ (i.e. $\phi(1) > 0$)
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{AR(2): the stationarity triangle}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $X_t = \phi_1X_{t-1} + \phi_2X_{t-2} + \varepsilon_t$ is stationary if and only if
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\phi_1 + \phi_2 < 1$, \quad $\phi_2 - \phi_1 < 1$, \quad $|\phi_2| < 1$
    \end{itemize}
    \item The roots are complex when $\phi_1^2 + 4\phi_2 < 0$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item then the ACF is a \textbf{damped cosine}: pseudo-cycles of average length $2\pi/\arccos\big(\phi_1/(2\sqrt{-\phi_2})\big)$
        \item damping factor per period: $\sqrt{-\phi_2}$, the modulus of the inverse roots
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Yule--Walker equations} for the ACF: multiply by $X_{t-h}$, take expectations, divide by $\gamma(0)$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\rho(1) = \phi_1 + \phi_2\rho(1)$, so $\rho(1) = \phi_1/(1 - \phi_2)$
        \item $\rho(h) = \phi_1\rho(h - 1) + \phi_2\rho(h - 2)$ for $h \ge 2$: the ACF obeys the same recursion as the process
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Three AR(2) processes and the sunspots}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch2_ar2.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item A: $\phi = (0.5, 0.3)$; B: $(1.0, -0.6)$; C: $(0.6, 0.5)$; Sunspots: Yule's AR(2), estimated in Section 10
    \item Middle: inverse roots $\lambda_i$; stationary means inside the circle
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch2\_ar\_models}{\qlurl{TSA_ch2_ar_models}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the AR(2) examples}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{A}: real roots $\ensuremath{-}2.84$ and $1.17$, both outside the circle: stationary
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\rho(1) = 0.5/0.7 = 0.714$, $\rho(2) = 0.5\rho(1) + 0.3 = 0.657$: slow, smooth decay
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{B}: complex roots $0.833 \pm 0.986\,i$, modulus $1.291 > 1$: stationary
    \begin{itemize}
        \item ACF: a wave with period 7.2 lags, damped by $0.775$ per lag: a \textbf{stochastic cycle}
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{C}: $\phi_1 + \phi_2 = 1.1 > 1$; one root $0.936 < 1$: \textbf{not} stationary (explosive)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item each coefficient is below 1, yet the process explodes: always check the roots, not the coefficients one by one
    \end{itemize}
    \item Complex roots are how linear models produce business cycles and the 11-year solar cycle
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The PACF of an AR($p$) cuts off after lag $p$}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\phi_{hh}$ = the last coefficient in the best linear prediction of $X_t$ from $X_{t-1}, \dots, X_{t-h}$ (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter1_stochastic_processes_stationarity.pdf}{Chapter 1})
    \begin{itemize}
        \item computed from the ACF by the Durbin--Levinson recursion (\refDurbin)
    \end{itemize}
    \item For an AR($p$) and $h > p$, the best predictor is the model itself: $\phi_1X_{t-1} + \dots + \phi_pX_{t-p}$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item so $\phi_{hh} = 0$ for $h > p$, and $\phi_{pp} = \phi_p$
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Identification rule}: ACF decays gradually, PACF has $p$ spikes and then stays inside the band: AR($p$)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item band for the sample PACF of an AR($p$) at lags $h > p$: $\pm 1.96/\sqrt{T}$
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: Autoregressive models}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item AR($p$): $\phi(L)X_t = c + \varepsilon_t$; stationary iff all roots of $\phi(z)$ lie outside the unit circle
    \item Mean $\mu = c/\phi(1)$; ACF from the Yule--Walker recursion, a mix of geometric decays and damped waves
    \item AR(1): $\rho(h) = \phi^h$, $\psi_j = \phi^j$, half-life $\ln 0.5/\ln\phi$
    \item PACF cuts off after lag $p$: the signature of an AR($p$)
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{Moving-average models}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{The MA($q$) model}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $X_t = \mu + \theta(L)\varepsilon_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t + \theta_1\varepsilon_{t-1} + \dots + \theta_q\varepsilon_{t-q}$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item a finite Wold sum: \textbf{always stationary}, for any $\theta$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Moments (derived in Seminar 1 and \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter1_stochastic_processes_stationarity.pdf}{Chapter 1}): with $\theta_0 = 1$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $E[X_t] = \mu$; $\gamma(h) = \sigma^2\sum_{j=0}^{q-h}\theta_j\theta_{j+h}$ for $0 \le h \le q$; $\gamma(h) = 0$ for $h > q$
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Identification rule}: the ACF \textbf{cuts off} after lag $q$; the PACF decays gradually
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the mirror image of the AR($p$) rule
        \item band for the sample ACF at lags $h > q$ (Bartlett): $\pm 1.96\sqrt{(1 + 2\sum_{j=1}^{q}\hat\rho(j)^2)/T}$, wider than $\pm 1.96/\sqrt{T}$
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{MA(1): $\theta = 0.8$ and $\theta = -0.8$}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch2_ma1.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $T = 300$; the ACF has one spike, the PACF decays (with alternating signs when $\theta > 0$)
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch2\_ma\_models}{\qlurl{TSA_ch2_ma_models}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the MA(1) correlograms}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Theory: $\rho(1) = \theta/(1 + \theta^2) = \pm 0.488$, $\rho(h) = 0$ for $h \ge 2$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item sample: $\hat\rho(1) = 0.56$ and $\ensuremath{-}0.51$
    \end{itemize}
    \item The PACF does not cut off: $\hat\phi_{22} = \ensuremath{-}0.23$ for $\theta = 0.8$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item an MA(1) is an AR($\infty$) (next slides), so every past value helps a little
    \end{itemize}
    \item An MA(1) remembers exactly one period: a shock today affects tomorrow and is then forgotten
    \item Economic examples: overlapping observations (Section 9), a measurement error, a bid--ask bounce in prices
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The largest autocorrelation of an MA(1)}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch2_ma1_rho.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\rho(1) = \theta/(1 + \theta^2)$ as a function of $\theta$
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch2\_ma\_models}{\qlurl{TSA_ch2_ma_models}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the curve $\rho(1)$}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Maximum $|\rho(1)| = 0.5$ at $\theta = \pm 1$: an MA(1) can never produce $|\rho(1)| > 0.5$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item if $\hat\rho(1) = 0.7$ and then nothing: not an MA(1); try an AR or an MA($q$) with more terms
    \end{itemize}
    \item $\theta = 0.5$ and $\theta = 2$ give the same $\rho(1) = 0.4$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item in general $\theta$ and $1/\theta$ give the same ACF (with $\sigma^2$ rescaled by $\theta^2$)
        \item the data cannot tell them apart: an \textbf{identification problem}
    \end{itemize}
    \item The convention that removes the ambiguity: invertibility, $|\theta| < 1$ (next slide)
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Invertibility}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item MA(1): $\varepsilon_t = X_t - \theta\varepsilon_{t-1}$; substitute repeatedly ($\mu = 0$):
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\varepsilon_t = X_t - \theta X_{t-1} + \theta^2X_{t-2} - \dots = \sum_{j \ge 0}(-\theta)^jX_{t-j}$, if $|\theta| < 1$
        \item an \textbf{AR($\infty$) representation}: $X_t = \theta X_{t-1} - \theta^2X_{t-2} + \dots + \varepsilon_t$
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Invertible}: the shocks can be recovered from the past of $X$; condition: all roots of $\theta(z) = 0$ outside the unit circle
    \begin{itemize}
        \item MA(1): $|\theta| < 1$; the same algebra as AR stationarity, applied to $\theta(z)$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Why we want it
    \begin{itemize}
        \item uniqueness: among $\theta$ and $1/\theta$ only one is invertible
        \item forecasting: the shocks $\varepsilon_t$ are computed from the data, so forecasts can use them
        \item software reports invertible estimates; a root near the circle signals over-differencing (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter1_stochastic_processes_stationarity.pdf}{Chapter 1})
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Worked example: $\theta = 2$ or $\theta = 0.5$?}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $X_t = \varepsilon_t + 2\varepsilon_{t-1}$, $\sigma^2 = 1$; and $Y_t = u_t + 0.5u_{t-1}$, $\mathrm{Var}(u_t) = 4$
    \item $X$: $\gamma(0) = 1 \cdot (1 + 4) = 5$, $\gamma(1) = 2 \cdot 1 = 2$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $Y$: $\gamma(0) = 4 \cdot (1 + 0.25) = 5$, $\gamma(1) = 0.5 \cdot 4 = 2$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Same mean, same autocovariances: with Gaussian shocks, the \textbf{same distribution}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item no amount of data separates them
    \end{itemize}
    \item Only $Y$ is invertible: $u_t = Y_t - 0.5Y_{t-1} + 0.25Y_{t-2} - \dots$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item for $X$, the same sum with weights $(-2)^j$ explodes
    \end{itemize}
    \item Rule: report the invertible version ($\theta = 0.5$, $\sigma^2 = 4$)
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: Moving-average models}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item MA($q$) is always stationary; its ACF cuts off after lag $q$, its PACF decays
    \item MA(1): $\rho(1) = \theta/(1 + \theta^2)$, at most $0.5$ in absolute value
    \item Invertible iff the roots of $\theta(z)$ lie outside the unit circle; then MA = AR($\infty$)
    \item $\theta$ and $1/\theta$ are observationally equivalent; we keep the invertible one
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{ARMA($p,q$) models}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{The ARMA($p,q$) model}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\phi(L)(X_t - \mu) = \theta(L)\varepsilon_t$, i.e.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $X_t = c + \phi_1X_{t-1} + \dots + \phi_pX_{t-p} + \varepsilon_t + \theta_1\varepsilon_{t-1} + \dots + \theta_q\varepsilon_{t-q}$, $c = \mu\,\phi(1)$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Three conditions (\refBD, Ch.~3)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{stationary and causal}: roots of $\phi(z)$ outside the unit circle; then $X_t - \mu = \psi(L)\varepsilon_t$, $\psi(L) = \theta(L)/\phi(L)$
        \item \textbf{invertible}: roots of $\theta(z)$ outside the unit circle; then $\pi(L)(X_t - \mu) = \varepsilon_t$, $\pi(L) = \phi(L)/\theta(L)$
        \item \textbf{no common factors}: $\phi(z)$ and $\theta(z)$ share no root
    \end{itemize}
    \item ARMA(1,1) can match a slowly decaying ACF that starts below $\phi$; a pure AR or MA would need many terms for it
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The $\psi$ weights and the impulse response}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item From $\phi(L)\psi(L) = \theta(L)$, match the coefficients of $L^j$:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\psi_0 = 1$, \quad $\psi_j = \theta_j + \sum_{i=1}^{\min(j,p)}\phi_i\psi_{j-i}$ \quad ($\theta_j = 0$ for $j > q$)
    \end{itemize}
    \item ARMA(1,1): $\psi_1 = \phi + \theta$, $\psi_j = \phi^{j-1}(\phi + \theta)$ for $j \ge 1$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item example $\phi = 0.7$, $\theta = 0.4$: $\psi_1 = 1.10$, $\psi_2 = 0.77$
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Impulse response}: $\psi_j = \partial X_{t+j}/\partial\varepsilon_t$, the effect of a unit shock after $j$ periods
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the same object drives the forecast errors (Section 7) and the impulse responses of VAR models (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter6_var_models_granger_causality.pdf}{Chapter 6})
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Impulse responses of four models}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch2_psi.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\psi_j$, $j = 0, \dots, 15$, from the recursion above
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch2\_arma\_acf}{\qlurl{TSA_ch2_arma_acf}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the impulse responses}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item AR(1): geometric decay $0.8^j$; the shock never vanishes completely, but fades fast enough for $\sum\psi_j^2 < \infty$
    \item AR(2) with complex roots: the response changes sign, $\psi_3 = \ensuremath{-}0.20$, $\psi_4 = \ensuremath{-}0.44$: a shock creates a cycle
    \item MA(2): exactly zero after two periods: finite memory
    \item ARMA(1,1): the MA term lifts the first response to $\psi_1 = 1.10 > 1$; afterwards the AR part takes over
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Moments of the ARMA(1,1)}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $X_t = \phi X_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t + \theta\varepsilon_{t-1}$, $|\phi| < 1$, $|\theta| < 1$, $\phi + \theta \ne 0$
    \item Variance, from $\gamma(0) = \sigma^2\sum_j\psi_j^2$:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\gamma(0) = \sigma^2\,\dfrac{1 + 2\phi\theta + \theta^2}{1 - \phi^2}$; for $\phi = 0.7$, $\theta = 0.4$, $\sigma^2 = 1$: $3.37$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Autocorrelations:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\rho(1) = \dfrac{(1 + \phi\theta)(\phi + \theta)}{1 + 2\phi\theta + \theta^2}$, \quad $\rho(h) = \phi\,\rho(h - 1)$ for $h \ge 2$
        \item example: $\rho(1) = 0.819$, $\rho(2) = 0.573$
    \end{itemize}
    \item The ACF decays like an AR(1) from lag 1 onwards, but $\rho(1) \ne \phi$: the MA part only moves the starting point
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Common factors: a model that is too large}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $X_t = 0.5X_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t - 0.5\varepsilon_{t-1}$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $(1 - 0.5L)X_t = (1 - 0.5L)\varepsilon_t$: cancel the factor, $X_t = \varepsilon_t$, white noise
    \end{itemize}
    \item In general $\phi = -\theta$ in an ARMA(1,1) gives white noise, for any value
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the likelihood is flat along the line $\phi = -\theta$: the parameters are not identified
    \end{itemize}
    \item Symptoms in software output
    \begin{itemize}
        \item large and opposite estimates, e.g. $\hat\phi = 0.9$, $\hat\theta = -0.88$, with huge standard errors
        \item a log-likelihood no better than the smaller model
    \end{itemize}
    \item Remedy: reduce $p$ and $q$ together; prefer the smallest model with white-noise residuals
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Identification: the ACF--PACF table}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{ACF} & \textbf{PACF} \\
\midrule
White noise & no significant lag & no significant lag \\
AR($p$) & decays (geometric or damped wave) & \textbf{cuts off} after lag $p$ \\
MA($q$) & \textbf{cuts off} after lag $q$ & decays \\
ARMA($p,q$) & decays after lag $q - p$ & decays after lag $p - q$ \\
Unit root (Ch.~3) & very slow, almost linear decay & $\hat\phi_{11} \approx 1$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}
    \item The table proposes \textbf{candidates}; the information criteria and the diagnostics decide (Sections 5--6)
    \item Mixed ARMA models are hard to spot by eye: both functions just decay
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Theoretical and sample ACF and PACF}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch2_patterns.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item AR(2) $\phi = (1.0, -0.6)$, MA(2) $\theta = (0.6, 0.3)$, ARMA(1,1) $\phi = 0.7$, $\theta = 0.4$; one simulated path of $T = 500$ each
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch2\_arma\_acf}{\qlurl{TSA_ch2_arma_acf}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the three patterns}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item AR(2): the PACF has two spikes, $\phi_{22} = \phi_2 = \ensuremath{-}0.60$, then zero; the ACF is a damped wave
    \begin{itemize}
        \item identification is easy: read $p$ from the PACF
    \end{itemize}
    \item MA(2): $\rho(1) = 0.538$, $\rho(2) = 0.207$, then zero; the PACF decays slowly
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the sample ACF at lag 2 is only just outside the band: with real data, MA(1) and MA(2) can look alike
    \end{itemize}
    \item ARMA(1,1): both decay; the ACF looks like an AR(1), the PACF has a second, smaller spike
    \begin{itemize}
        \item an analyst who reads only the PACF would choose AR(2) or AR(3): close, but more parameters
    \end{itemize}
    \item Sample correlograms are noisy even with $T = 500$; with 100 quarterly observations, much more so
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: ARMA models}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item ARMA($p,q$): $\phi(L)(X_t - \mu) = \theta(L)\varepsilon_t$; causal if $\phi(z)$ has roots outside the circle, invertible if $\theta(z)$ has
    \item $\psi$ weights by the recursion $\psi_j = \theta_j + \sum\phi_i\psi_{j-i}$: the impulse response
    \item No common factors; a flat likelihood and opposite estimates signal one
    \item ACF cuts off: MA; PACF cuts off: AR; both decay: ARMA
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{Estimation}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{Three estimators}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Yule--Walker} (method of moments, \refYule; \refWalker): replace $\rho(h)$ by $\hat\rho(h)$ in the Yule--Walker equations
    \begin{itemize}
        \item pure AR only; fast; always gives a stationary model; less precise when roots are near the circle
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Conditional least squares}: minimise $\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2$, treating the first values as fixed
    \begin{itemize}
        \item AR($p$): ordinary least squares (OLS) of $X_t$ on $1, X_{t-1}, \dots, X_{t-p}$
        \item MA and ARMA: the residuals $\varepsilon_t = X_t - \mu - \theta\varepsilon_{t-1} - \dots$ are computed recursively from $\varepsilon_0 = 0$; numerical minimisation
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Exact Gaussian maximum likelihood} (MLE): maximise the joint density of $(X_1, \dots, X_T)$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item uses the first observations too; the default of \texttt{statsmodels} \texttt{ARIMA} (Kalman filter, \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter10_state_space_kalman_markov_switching.pdf}{Chapter 10})
    \end{itemize}
    \item In large samples all three agree for pure AR models; MLE is the reference for MA and ARMA
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Yule--Walker for an AR($p$)}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.64\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item For $h = 1, \dots, p$: $\rho(h) = \phi_1\rho(h - 1) + \dots + \phi_p\rho(h - p)$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item in matrix form $R\,\phi = \rho$, $R_{ij} = \rho(|i - j|)$; $\phi = (\phi_1, \dots, \phi_p)^\top$, $\rho = (\rho(1), \dots, \rho(p))^\top$
        \item $R$: the $p \times p$ matrix of autocorrelations; the hat marks the sample version
        \item estimator $\hat\phi = \hat R^{-1}\hat\rho$; noise variance $\hat\sigma^2 = \hat\gamma(0)(1 - \hat\phi^\top\hat\rho)$
    \end{itemize}
    \item AR(2) by Cramer's rule:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\hat\phi_1 = \dfrac{\hat\rho_1(1 - \hat\rho_2)}{1 - \hat\rho_1^2}$, \quad $\hat\phi_2 = \dfrac{\hat\rho_2 - \hat\rho_1^2}{1 - \hat\rho_1^2}$
        \item $\hat\phi_2$ is the sample PACF at lag 2 (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter1_stochastic_processes_stationarity.pdf}{Chapter 1})
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.32\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.46\textheight]{ch2_gilbert_walker.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{Gilbert Walker (1868--1958), who extended Yule's method in 1931}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gilbert_Walker.jpg}{Photo: unknown author (1925); public domain; Wikimedia Commons}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Worked example: Yule--Walker on Romanian GDP growth}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Annual growth of real GDP, 2000Q1--2026Q2 (Section 9): $\hat\rho(1) = 0.62$, $\hat\rho(2) = 0.40$, $\hat\gamma(0) = 18.95$
    \item Determinant $1 - \hat\rho_1^2 = 0.620$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\hat\phi_1 = 0.62\,(1 - 0.40)/0.620 = 0.600$
        \item $\hat\phi_2 = (0.40 - 0.62^2)/0.620 = 0.027$
    \end{itemize}
    \item $\hat\sigma^2 = 18.95\,(1 - \hat\phi_1\hat\rho_1 - \hat\phi_2\hat\rho_2) = 11.74$
    \item $\hat\phi_2 \approx 0$: the second lag adds nothing, AR(1) would do
    \begin{itemize}
        \item but is an AR model the right family at all? Section 9 shows that an MA(3) fits better
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Maximum likelihood}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Gaussian likelihood by the \textbf{prediction-error decomposition}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $f(x_1, \dots, x_T) = \prod_t f(x_t \mid x_{t-1}, \dots, x_1)$; each factor is $N(\hat x_{t|t-1}, v_t)$
        \item $\ln L = -\tfrac12\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big[\ln(2\pi v_t) + (x_t - \hat x_{t|t-1})^2/v_t\big]$
        \item $\hat x_{t|t-1}$: one-step prediction; $v_t$: its error variance, larger for the first observations
    \end{itemize}
    \item AR(1) by hand: $X_1 \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2/(1 - \phi^2))$, then $X_t \mid X_{t-1} \sim N(c + \phi X_{t-1}, \sigma^2)$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item dropping the first factor gives conditional least squares
    \end{itemize}
    \item Standard errors (se) from the curvature of $\ln L$; asymptotically
    \begin{itemize}
        \item AR(1): $\mathrm{se}(\hat\phi) \approx \sqrt{(1 - \phi^2)/T}$; MA(1): $\mathrm{se}(\hat\theta) \approx \sqrt{(1 - \theta^2)/T}$
        \item $t$-ratios $\hat\phi/\mathrm{se}$ compared with $\pm 1.96$, as in regression
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Sampling distributions of the estimators}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch2_estimators.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item 400 simulated samples of $T = 100$ each; left: AR(1) with $\phi = 0.9$; right: MA(1) with $\theta = 0.5$
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch2\_estimation}{\qlurl{TSA_ch2_estimation}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the estimator comparison}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item AR(1), $\phi = 0.9$: means 0.853 (Yule--Walker), 0.864 (conditional least squares), 0.866 (MLE)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item all three are biased downwards; the textbook approximation of the least squares bias is $-(1 + 3\phi)/T = \ensuremath{-}0.037$
        \item Yule--Walker is the most biased near the unit circle
    \end{itemize}
    \item Standard deviations 0.056, 0.055, 0.054, above the asymptotic 0.044
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the distribution is skewed to the left: asymptotic intervals are optimistic near $\phi = 1$
    \end{itemize}
    \item MA(1), $\theta = 0.5$: conditional least squares 0.504 (sd 0.097), MLE 0.506 (sd 0.098); asymptotic sd 0.087
    \item Practical rule: use MLE; Yule--Walker only for quick starting values or for teaching
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: Estimation}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Yule--Walker: moments, pure AR, $\hat\phi = \hat R^{-1}\hat\rho$
    \item Conditional least squares: OLS for AR, a recursion for MA
    \item Exact Gaussian MLE: the prediction-error decomposition; the standard in software
    \item Persistent AR coefficients are biased downwards in small samples
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{Model selection and diagnostics}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{Information criteria}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.64\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Fit improves with every parameter; the criteria charge a \textbf{penalty} per parameter
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $k$ = number of estimated parameters ($\phi$, $\theta$, $\mu$, $\sigma^2$), $\ln L$ = maximised log-likelihood
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{AIC} $= -2\ln L + 2k$ (\refAkaike)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{AICc} $= \mathrm{AIC} + 2k(k + 1)/(T - k - 1)$, for small $T$ (\refHT)
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{BIC} $= -2\ln L + k\ln T$ (\refSchwarz)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\ln T > 2$ once $T \ge 8$: BIC prefers smaller models
    \end{itemize}
    \item Choose the model with the \textbf{smallest} value; compare only models fitted to the same observations
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.32\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.44\textheight]{ch2_hirotugu_akaike.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{Hirotugu Akaike (1927--2009), Institute of Statistical Mathematics, Tokyo}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Akaike.jpg}{Photo: The Institute of Statistical Mathematics (2017); CC BY-SA 4.0; Wikimedia Commons}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{AIC or BIC?}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{BIC is consistent}: if the true model is among the candidates, BIC finds it with probability $\to 1$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item but it may choose a model that is too small when $T$ is small
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{AIC targets forecasting}: it estimates the expected out-of-sample fit (Kullback--Leibler distance)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item it overfits with positive probability, even with large $T$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Practice (\refFPP, Ch.~9; \refHK)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item automatic searches (\texttt{auto.arima}, \texttt{pmdarima}) minimise AICc over a grid of $(p, q)$
        \item when AIC and BIC disagree, keep both candidates and let the diagnostics and the forecasts decide
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{How often AIC and BIC find the true order}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch2_ic.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item True model AR(2), $\phi = (0.5, 0.25)$; AR($p$), $p = 0, \dots, 6$, fitted by OLS on the same sample; 500 samples per panel
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch2\_selection}{\qlurl{TSA_ch2_selection}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the selection experiment}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $T = 100$: AIC finds $p = 2$ in 54.4\% of samples, BIC in 47.4\%
    \begin{itemize}
        \item BIC chooses too small a model in 50.4\% (the small $\phi_2 = 0.25$ is hard to detect); AIC too large in 24.8\%
    \end{itemize}
    \item $T = 1000$: BIC 98.6\%, AIC 74.4\%
    \begin{itemize}
        \item BIC is consistent; AIC still overfits in 25.6\% of samples
    \end{itemize}
    \item Neither criterion is a proof: with quarterly macro data ($T \approx 100$) the order is uncertain
    \item Overfitting costs little in forecasts; underfitting leaves correlation in the residuals, which the diagnostics catch
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Residual diagnostics}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item If the model is right, the residuals $\hat\varepsilon_t$ behave like white noise
    \begin{itemize}
        \item plot them: no pattern, no change of variance, no isolated huge values
        \item residual ACF inside $\pm 1.96/\sqrt{T}$, except about 1 lag in 20
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Ljung--Box} on residuals (\refLB): $Q^*(m) = T(T + 2)\sum_{h=1}^{m}\hat\rho_{\hat\varepsilon}(h)^2/(T - h)$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item under $H_0$ (correct model) $Q^*(m) \approx \chi^2(m - p - q)$ (\refBP): estimating $p + q$ coefficients uses up $p + q$ degrees of freedom
        \item choose $m$ well above $p + q$: $m = 10$ for annual or quarterly data, $m = 2s$ for seasonal data (\refFPP)
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Normality}: Jarque--Bera (\refJB) $\mathrm{JB} = \frac{T}{6}\big(S^2 + (K - 3)^2/4\big) \approx \chi^2(2)$; QQ plot
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $S$ = skewness, $K$ = kurtosis (0 and 3 for the Normal distribution); reject normality at 5\% if $\mathrm{JB} > 5.99$, the 95\% quantile of $\chi^2(2)$
        \item non-Normal residuals do not bias $\hat\phi$, but they make Normal intervals wrong
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Squared residuals}: Ljung--Box on $\hat\varepsilon_t^2$ detects volatility clustering (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter5_conditional_volatility_garch.pdf}{Chapter 5})
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Why $m - p - q$ degrees of freedom}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch2_lb_df.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Ljung--Box at 5\% on the residuals of the \textbf{true} model; 1\,000 samples of AR(1), half as many of ARMA(1,1)
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch2\_selection}{\qlurl{TSA_ch2_selection}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the degrees-of-freedom experiment}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item With $m = 10$ degrees of freedom the test rejects too rarely: 3.2\% (AR(1)) and 1.4\% (ARMA(1,1)) instead of 5\%
    \begin{itemize}
        \item residuals are fitted to look uncorrelated at the first lags: their ACF is smaller than that of true white noise
    \end{itemize}
    \item With $m - p - q$: 4.8\% and 3.4\%, close to the nominal 5\%
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the correction matters most when $p + q$ is large relative to $m$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Software (\texttt{acorr\_ljungbox}) uses $m$ by default: pass \texttt{model\_df = p + q}
    \item Wrong degrees of freedom make a bad model look acceptable
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: Model selection and diagnostics}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item AIC $= -2\ln L + 2k$, BIC $= -2\ln L + k\ln T$; smallest wins; BIC picks smaller models
    \item BIC is consistent, AIC aims at forecasting and overfits sometimes
    \item Residuals: plot, ACF, Ljung--Box with $m - p - q$ degrees of freedom, Jarque--Bera, Ljung--Box on squares
    \item A model passes when its residuals are white noise; normality matters for the intervals
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{Forecasting with ARMA models}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{The optimal forecast}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Forecast of $X_{T+h}$ made at time $T$: $\hat X_{T+h|T} = E[X_{T+h} \mid X_T, X_{T-1}, \dots]$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item it minimises the mean squared error (MSE) among all functions of the past
    \end{itemize}
    \item Recipe: write the model at $T + h$ and replace
    \begin{itemize}
        \item future shocks $\varepsilon_{T+j}$, $j \ge 1$, by 0
        \item future values $X_{T+j}$ by their forecasts; past values and past residuals stay as they are
    \end{itemize}
    \item AR(1): $\hat X_{T+h|T} = \mu + \phi^h(X_T - \mu)$: \textbf{mean reversion} at the speed $\phi$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item MA($q$): $\hat X_{T+h|T} = \mu$ for $h > q$: after $q$ steps the model knows nothing beyond the mean
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Forecast errors and intervals}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item From the causal form $X_{T+h} = \mu + \sum_j\psi_j\varepsilon_{T+h-j}$:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item error $e_{T+h} = X_{T+h} - \hat X_{T+h|T} = \varepsilon_{T+h} + \psi_1\varepsilon_{T+h-1} + \dots + \psi_{h-1}\varepsilon_{T+1}$
        \item variance $\sigma_h^2 = \sigma^2(1 + \psi_1^2 + \dots + \psi_{h-1}^2)$, increasing in $h$
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{95\% interval}: $\hat X_{T+h|T} \pm 1.96\,\sigma_h$ (Gaussian shocks)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $h = 1$: $\pm 1.96\,\sigma$; $h \to \infty$: $\sigma_h^2 \to \gamma(0)$, the unconditional variance
    \end{itemize}
    \item What the interval leaves out
    \begin{itemize}
        \item parameter uncertainty ($\hat\phi$ instead of $\phi$), model uncertainty, fat tails: real coverage is usually below 95\%
    \end{itemize}
    \item Errors of forecasts made at the same time for horizons $h$ and $h + 1$ are correlated: they share shocks
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Worked example: forecasting an AR(1)}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $X_t = 2 + 0.8X_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$, $\sigma^2 = 1$, $\mu = 10$; last value $X_T = 12$
    \item Point forecasts
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\hat X_{T+1} = 10 + 0.8 \cdot 2 = 11.60$; $\hat X_{T+2} = 10 + 0.64 \cdot 2 = 11.28$; $\hat X_{T+10} = 10.21$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Error variances: $\sigma_1^2 = 1$, $\sigma_2^2 = 1 + 0.8^2 = 1.64$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item 95\% intervals: $h = 1$: $[9.64, 13.56]$; $h = 2$: $[8.77, 13.79]$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Long run: forecast $\to 10$, standard deviation $\to \sqrt{\gamma(0)} = 1.67$
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Mean reversion in forecasts}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch2_forecast_theory.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Start at $X_T = 3$, $\mu = 0$, $\sigma = 1$; dashed: the unconditional band $\mu \pm 1.96\,\sigma_X$
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch2\_forecasting}{\qlurl{TSA_ch2_forecasting}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the forecast paths}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\phi = 0.9$: slow reversion; after 5 periods the forecast is still 1.77, standard error 1.85
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the interval approaches $\pm 1.96 \times 2.29$ only after many periods
    \end{itemize}
    \item $\phi = 0.5$: after 5 periods the forecast is 0.094, practically the mean
    \item MA(1): one informative step ($\theta\varepsilon_T = 1.2$), then the mean; the interval jumps to its long-run width at $h = 2$
    \item A stationary model always forecasts a return to the mean: useful for spreads and growth rates, misleading if the mean shifts
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: Forecasting}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\hat X_{T+h|T}$: replace future shocks by 0 and future values by forecasts
    \item Error variance $\sigma^2\sum_{j<h}\psi_j^2$; intervals widen up to $\pm 1.96\sqrt{\gamma(0)}$
    \item Forecasts revert to $\mu$; MA($q$) forecasts equal $\mu$ beyond $q$ steps
    \item Intervals ignore parameter and model uncertainty
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{The Box--Jenkins method}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{George Box and Gwilym Jenkins}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.62\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{George E. P. Box} (1919--2013), statistician, University of Wisconsin--Madison
    \begin{itemize}
        \item ``All models are wrong, but some are useful''
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Gwilym M. Jenkins} (1932--1982), statistician, Lancaster University
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textit{Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control}, 1970; fourth edition with Reinsel: \refBJ
    \end{itemize}
    \item Their contribution: not new models, but a \textbf{method}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item a loop of identification, estimation and checking that anyone can apply
        \item Box--Pierce (1970) and Ljung--Box (1978) come from this programme
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.34\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.50\textheight]{ch2_george_box.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{George E. P. Box}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:GeorgeEPBox.jpg}{Photo: DavidMCEddy; CC BY-SA 3.0; Wikimedia Commons}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The Box--Jenkins loop}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=0.55cm and 0.5cm, font=\footnotesize,
  bx/.style={draw=MainBlue, rounded corners, fill=MainBlue!8, align=center, minimum height=0.95cm, text width=2.35cm},
  ar/.style={-{Stealth[length=2mm]}, thick, MainBlue}]
\node[bx] (a) {0. Prepare\\{\scriptsize plot, transform, make stationary}};
\node[bx, right=of a] (b) {1. Identify\\{\scriptsize ACF, PACF: candidates $(p,q)$}};
\node[bx, right=of b] (c) {2. Estimate\\{\scriptsize MLE; AIC, BIC}};
\node[bx, right=of c] (d) {3. Check\\{\scriptsize residuals, Ljung--Box, roots}};
\node[bx, below=0.9cm of d, fill=Forest!10, draw=Forest] (e) {4. Forecast\\{\scriptsize points and intervals}};
\draw[ar] (a) -- (b); \draw[ar] (b) -- (c); \draw[ar] (c) -- (d);
\draw[ar, Forest] (d) -- node[right, font=\scriptsize, text=Forest] {passes} (e);
\draw[ar, IDAred] (d.north) -- ++(0, 0.5) -| node[pos=0.25, above, font=\scriptsize, text=IDAred] {fails: back to identification} (b.north);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Step 0 is \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter1_stochastic_processes_stationarity.pdf}{Chapters 1} and \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter3_unit_roots_arima_models.pdf}{3}: logs, differences, unit-root tests; ARMA needs a stationary series
    \item The loop ends with the smallest model whose residuals are white noise and whose roots are well inside the admissible region
    \item Out-of-sample checks (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter0_introduction.pdf}{Chapter 0}: training and test samples) complete the method
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{Case study: Romanian GDP growth}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{The data}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.60\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Romanian real GDP, chain-linked volumes (2010 prices), quarterly, not seasonally adjusted; Eurostat, \texttt{namq\_10\_gdp}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the national source: the National Institute of Statistics (INS)
    \end{itemize}
    \item Annual growth $y_t = 100\,(\ln Y_t - \ln Y_{t-4})$, in \%: removes the season (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter1_stochastic_processes_stationarity.pdf}{Chapter 1})
    \begin{itemize}
        \item 2000Q1--2026Q2: $T = 106$ quarters, mean 3.29\%, standard deviation 4.35\%
        \item extremes: $\ensuremath{-}9.9\%$ in 2020Q2, $+12.5\%$ in 2004Q4; last value $\ensuremath{-}2.0\%$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Stationary? No trend in the growth rate; a formal test is in \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter3_unit_roots_arima_models.pdf}{Chapter 3}
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.36\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.42\textheight]{ch2_ins_bucharest_2009.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{The National Institute of Statistics, Bucharest}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Institutul_Na\%C8\%9Bional_de_Statistic\%C4\%83.jpg}{Photo: Dan Mihai Pitea (2009); CC BY-SA 3.0; Wikimedia Commons}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Step 1: identification}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch2_gdp_ident.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Annual growth of Romanian real GDP, its ACF and PACF with $\pm 1.96/\sqrt{T} = \pm 0.19$
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch2\_gdp\_case}{\qlurl{TSA_ch2_gdp_case}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the correlograms of GDP growth}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item ACF: $0.62$, $0.40$, $0.21$, then $\ensuremath{-}0.01$ at lag 4: \textbf{cuts off after lag 3}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item candidate: MA(3)
    \end{itemize}
    \item PACF: $0.62$ at lag 1, then small, except $0.32$ at lag 5
    \begin{itemize}
        \item candidate: AR(1); lag 5 may be chance or a remnant of the season
    \end{itemize}
    \item Why MA(3)? $y_t$ is the sum of four quarterly growth rates, $y_t \approx g_t + g_{t-1} + g_{t-2} + g_{t-3}$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item if $g_t$ is close to white noise (Seminar 2, B2), consecutive annual rates share three quarters: an MA(3) by construction
    \end{itemize}
    \item Ljung--Box $Q^*(8) = 64.9$ on the series itself: strongly autocorrelated, so a model is needed
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Step 2: estimation and information criteria}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & $k$ & $\ln L$ & \textbf{AIC} & \textbf{BIC} & $\hat\sigma$ & \textbf{LB p-value} \\
\midrule
ARMA(0,0) & 2 & $\ensuremath{-}305.83$ & 615.66 & 620.99 & 4.33 & $<$\,0.001 \\
ARMA(1,0) & 3 & $\ensuremath{-}279.67$ & 565.33 & 573.32 & 3.38 & 0.023 \\
ARMA(2,0) & 4 & $\ensuremath{-}279.66$ & 567.32 & 577.98 & 3.38 & 0.037 \\
ARMA(1,1) & 4 & $\ensuremath{-}279.66$ & 567.32 & 577.98 & 3.38 & 0.013 \\
ARMA(0,3) & 5 & $\ensuremath{-}270.02$ & 550.04 & 563.36 & 3.07 & 0.375 \\
ARMA(1,3) & 6 & $\ensuremath{-}268.48$ & 548.97 & 564.95 & 3.02 & 0.648 \\
ARMA(2,3) & 7 & $\ensuremath{-}267.94$ & 549.89 & 568.53 & 3.00 & 0.543 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Exact Gaussian MLE on the same 106 quarters; LB = Ljung--Box $Q^*(8)$ on the residuals, $8 - p - q$ degrees of freedom; full grid $p, q \le 3$ in the Quantlet
    \item \textbf{BIC} chooses MA(3); \textbf{AIC} chooses ARMA(1,3), lower by only 1.07
    \item AR(1), the PACF candidate, leaves autocorrelation: LB p-value 0.023
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the estimated MA(3)}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\hat y_t = 3.17 + \hat\varepsilon_t + 0.834\,\hat\varepsilon_{t-1} + 0.675\,\hat\varepsilon_{t-2} + 0.591\,\hat\varepsilon_{t-3}$, $\hat\sigma = 3.07$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item standard errors: 1.03 (mean), 0.083, 0.102, 0.082: all three MA terms are significant
    \end{itemize}
    \item The $\hat\theta_j$ decline from 0.834 to 0.591: close to, but below, the overlap pattern $(1, 1, 1)$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $(1, 1, 1)$ would put roots on the unit circle; the smallest root modulus here is 1.17 $> 1$: invertible
    \end{itemize}
    \item ARMA(1,3): $\hat\theta_1 = 1.019 > 1$, yet the roots have modulus at least 1.10: still invertible
    \begin{itemize}
        \item for $q > 1$, invertibility is read from the roots, not from single coefficients
        \item $\hat\phi = \ensuremath{-}0.284$ (se 0.143): one extra parameter for little gain; BIC drops it
    \end{itemize}
    \item Mean growth 3.17\% per year, but with a standard error of 1.03: overlapping data carry less information than $T$ suggests
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Step 3: diagnostics of the MA(3)}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch2_gdp_diag.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Residuals, their ACF, Ljung--Box p-values for $m = 4, \dots, 16$ with $m - 3$ degrees of freedom, Normal QQ plot
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch2\_gdp\_case}{\qlurl{TSA_ch2_gdp_case}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the MA(3) diagnostics}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item No residual autocorrelation: $Q^*(8) = 5.35$ on 5 degrees of freedom, p = 0.375; $Q^*(16)$: p = 0.525
    \begin{itemize}
        \item every p-value in the chart is above 0.12; with 8 instead of 5 degrees of freedom, p would be 0.720, too reassuring
    \end{itemize}
    \item Not Normal: Jarque--Bera 39.0, p $<$\,0.001; skewness \ensuremath{-}0.75, kurtosis 5.61
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the largest residual: $\ensuremath{-}11.4$ in 2020Q2, \ensuremath{-}3.89 standard deviations: the pandemic lockdown
    \end{itemize}
    \item Squared residuals: Ljung--Box p = 0.779, no volatility clustering at this frequency
    \item Verdict: the MA(3) captures the dependence; the Normal intervals understate the risk of recessions
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Step 4: forecasts}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch2_gdp_forecast.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item MA(3) (BIC) and AR(1) forecasts for 2026Q3--2028Q2, with 95\% intervals
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch2\_gdp\_case}{\qlurl{TSA_ch2_gdp_case}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the GDP forecasts}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item MA(3): $\ensuremath{-}0.14$, $1.81$, $2.77$, then the mean $3.17$\% from the fourth quarter on
    \begin{itemize}
        \item exactly the MA($q$) rule: after $q = 3$ steps the model only knows the mean
    \end{itemize}
    \item AR(1): a smooth return to its mean, 2.99\% after 8 quarters (mean 3.12\%)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the two models agree in the short run and differ in how fast they forget the recent slowdown
    \end{itemize}
    \item Intervals: $[\ensuremath{-}6.1, 5.9]$ one quarter ahead, $[\ensuremath{-}6.3, 12.7]$ from four quarters on: $\pm 6.0$ and $\pm 9.5$ percentage points
    \item A univariate model cannot anticipate a turning point; it tells us how unusual the next value would be
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: Romanian GDP growth}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Annual growth of quarterly GDP: ACF cuts off after lag 3, MA(3) by BIC, ARMA(1,3) by AIC
    \item The MA(3) is the overlap of four quarters: the data structure explains the model
    \item White-noise residuals but fat tails (2020): intervals are too narrow in crises
    \item Forecasts reach the mean after three quarters
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\section{More real series}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{Romanian inflation: an AR(2) forecast}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch2_inflation.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item HICP (harmonised index of consumer prices, Eurostat), 12-month rate in \%, 260 months to August 2026; AR order chosen by BIC among $p \le 6$
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch2\_real\_series}{\qlurl{TSA_ch2_real_series}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the inflation model}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{itemize}
    \item BIC: 495.7 for AR(1), 469.7 for AR(2), 473.4 for AR(3): AR(2)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\hat\phi_1 = 1.320$ (0.057), $\hat\phi_2 = \ensuremath{-}0.344$ (0.055); $\hat\phi_1 + \hat\phi_2 = 0.976$, largest inverse root 0.963
    \end{itemize}
    \item Very close to a unit root: is inflation stationary at all? The test is in \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter3_unit_roots_arima_models.pdf}{Chapter 3}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the estimated mean, $5.16\%$ (se 1.35), is the average of 2005--2026, above the BNR target of 2.5\% $\pm$ 1 p.p.
    \end{itemize}
    \item Forecast: from 6.09\% to 5.44\% next month and 5.13\% in August 2028; 95\% interval $[\ensuremath{-}0.6, 10.9]$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the model reverts to its historical mean, not to the target: it knows nothing about monetary policy
    \end{itemize}
    \item Diagnostics fail: Ljung--Box $Q^*(12) = 71.6$, p $<$\,0.001: correlation at lag 12 (base effects of the 12-month rate), a job for \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter4_seasonality_forecasting.pdf}{Chapter 4}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Daily returns: BET and EUR/RON}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch2_returns.pdf}
\end{center}

\end{itemize}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the AR(1) for daily returns}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
 & \textbf{BET} & \textbf{EUR/RON} \\
\midrule
Observations & 6\,670 & 5\,352 \\
$\hat\phi$ (se) & $0.109$ (0.005) & $0.170$ (0.006) \\
$t$-ratio & 20.9 & 30.6 \\
$R^2$ (\%) & 1.2 & 2.9 \\
LB $Q^*(10)$ residuals, 9 df (p) & 29.7 ($<$\,0.001) & 61.5 ($<$\,0.001) \\
LB $Q^*(10)$ squared residuals & 2496 & 2351 \\
Kurtosis of residuals & 14.0 & 17.0 \\
BIC choice, $p, q \le 2$ & ARMA(1,0) & ARMA(2,1) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Highly significant $\hat\phi$, but $R^2$ of 1--3\%: \textbf{statistically} real, \textbf{economically} small after trading costs
    \item Positive $\hat\phi$: slow price adjustment (BET), a managed exchange rate (EUR/RON)
    \item Squared residuals and kurtosis: the mean is modelled, the variance is not; ARMA + GARCH in \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter5_conditional_volatility_garch.pdf}{Chapter 5}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Case study: Yule (1927) and the sunspots}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \refYule{} fitted the first autoregression: Wolfer's yearly sunspot numbers, 1749--1924
    \begin{itemize}
        \item until then, cycles were modelled as sums of sine waves (periodogram)
        \item Yule: a ``pendulum bombarded by peas'': a damped oscillator kicked by random shocks
    \end{itemize}
    \item Our least squares AR(2) on the same years (176 observations, statsmodels data):
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\hat\phi_1 = 1.336$, $\hat\phi_2 = \ensuremath{-}0.650$: complex roots, modulus of the inverse roots 0.806
        \item implied period $2\pi/\arccos(\hat\phi_1/(2\sqrt{-\hat\phi_2})) = 10.57$ years: the solar cycle, from two coefficients
    \end{itemize}
    \item \refWalker{} generalised the equations to AR($p$): the Yule--Walker equations
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the start of parametric time series analysis
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The sunspots: AR(2) and the information criteria}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\textwidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{tsa_ch2_sunspots.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-0.25cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Yearly sunspot numbers, 1700--2008 (309 years); AR($p$) by MLE on the full sample
\end{itemize}
\quantlet{TSA\_ch2\_real\_series}{\qlurl{TSA_ch2_real_series}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Interpreting the sunspot models}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Full-sample AR(2): $\hat\phi = (1.391, \ensuremath{-}0.689)$, close to Yule's; it explains 83\% of the variance one year ahead
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the one-step predictions follow the cycle, but lag behind at the peaks
    \end{itemize}
    \item AIC and BIC both choose $p = 9$ over $p \le 10$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the cycle is asymmetric (fast rise, slow decay), which a linear AR(2) cannot reproduce
    \end{itemize}
    \item Lesson: two parameters capture the essence; more lags capture details; nonlinearity is beyond ARMA
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Case study: forecasting competitions}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \refMH: the M3 competition, 3003 series (yearly, quarterly, monthly, other), 24 methods
    \begin{itemize}
        \item forecasts compared out of sample, on several accuracy measures and horizons
    \end{itemize}
    \item Conclusions confirmed from the earlier M-competitions
    \begin{itemize}
        \item statistically sophisticated methods do not necessarily forecast better than simple ones
        \item the ranking depends on the accuracy measure and on the horizon; combinations of methods do well
    \end{itemize}
    \item Consequences for ARMA
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the Box--Jenkins loop must end with an out-of-sample comparison against simple benchmarks (mean, last value, exponential smoothing from \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter0_introduction.pdf}{Chapter 0})
        \item Seminar 2, C1 runs this comparison for Romanian inflation
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: More real series}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Inflation: AR(2) near a unit root; reverts to the historical mean; lag-12 residual correlation
    \item Daily returns: significant but tiny AR effects; the variance needs GARCH
    \item Sunspots: Yule's AR(2) gives the 11-year cycle from complex roots
    \item Forecasting competitions: always compare with simple benchmarks
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{Possible contribution of AI}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{Possible contribution of AI}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Code}: a first draft of a loop that fits ARMA($p,q$) on a grid, tabulates AIC and BIC, and runs the residual tests
    \item \textbf{Explanation}: a second derivation of the ACF of an ARMA(1,1), or of why the PACF of an MA decays
    \item \textbf{Exploration}: the same Box--Jenkins loop on many series (GDP growth of all EU countries) to compare persistence
    \item Example prompt
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \aiprompt{Write Python code with statsmodels that fits ARMA(p,q), p,q <= 3, to Romanian annual GDP growth from Eurostat, reports AIC, BIC and the Ljung-Box p-value with model\_df = p + q, and forecasts 8 quarters from the BIC model.}
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Checks you must run}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item The sign convention of $\theta$ and $\phi$ in the software ($\theta(L) = 1 + \theta L$ in statsmodels, $1 - \theta L$ in some books)
    \item Intercept or mean: the \texttt{const} of \texttt{ARIMA} is the mean $\mu$, not $c$
    \item Ljung--Box degrees of freedom on residuals ($m - p - q$), and that all models are compared on the same sample
    \item Roots of both polynomials, not the size of single coefficients
    \item That the series is stationary before an ARMA is fitted (\tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter3_unit_roots_arima_models.pdf}{Chapter 3}), and that forecasts are compared with simple benchmarks
    \item Every cited reference: it must exist; check the DOI
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{Summary}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{Key takeaways}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item ARMA($p,q$) replaces the infinite Wold sum by a ratio of two short polynomials, $\theta(L)/\phi(L)$
    \item Stationarity: roots of $\phi(z)$ outside the unit circle; invertibility: roots of $\theta(z)$ outside; no common factors
    \item ACF cuts off: MA; PACF cuts off: AR; both decay: ARMA
    \item Estimate by MLE, choose by AIC/BIC, check residuals with Ljung--Box on $m - p - q$ degrees of freedom
    \item Forecasts revert to the mean; intervals widen to $\pm 1.96\sqrt{\gamma(0)}$ and ignore parameter uncertainty
    \item Real data: GDP growth is an MA(3) by construction; inflation is near a unit root; returns need GARCH
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Key formulas}
\itemsize{\small}
{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
\textbf{Quantity} & \textbf{Formula} \\
\midrule
ARMA($p,q$) & $\phi(L)(X_t - \mu) = \theta(L)\varepsilon_t$, \quad $\psi(L) = \theta(L)/\phi(L)$ \\
AR(1) & $\mu = c/(1 - \phi)$, \quad $\gamma(0) = \sigma^2/(1 - \phi^2)$, \quad $\rho(h) = \phi^h$ \\
AR(2) & $\rho(1) = \phi_1/(1 - \phi_2)$, \quad $\rho(h) = \phi_1\rho(h - 1) + \phi_2\rho(h - 2)$ \\
MA(1) & $\rho(1) = \theta/(1 + \theta^2)$, \quad $\rho(h) = 0$, $h \ge 2$; invertible $|\theta| < 1$ \\
ARMA(1,1) & $\psi_j = \phi^{j-1}(\phi + \theta)$, \quad $\rho(h) = \phi\rho(h - 1)$, $h \ge 2$ \\
Yule--Walker & $\hat\phi = \hat R^{-1}\hat\rho$, \quad $\hat\sigma^2 = \hat\gamma(0)(1 - \hat\phi^\top\hat\rho)$ \\
Criteria & $\mathrm{AIC} = -2\ln L + 2k$, \quad $\mathrm{BIC} = -2\ln L + k\ln T$ \\
Residuals & $Q^*(m) \sim \chi^2(m - p - q)$ \\
Forecast & $\hat X_{T+h|T} \pm 1.96\,\sigma\sqrt{\textstyle\sum_{j=0}^{h-1}\psi_j^2}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Self-assessment}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question}: is $X_t = 1.2X_{t-1} - 0.32X_{t-2} + \varepsilon_t$ stationary?
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{Answer}: $1 - 1.2z + 0.32z^2 = (1 - 0.8z)(1 - 0.4z)$, roots 1.25 and 2.5, both outside the circle: yes
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question}: the ACF of a series has one spike $\hat\rho(1) = -0.45$ and the PACF decays. Which model?
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{Answer}: MA(1) with $\theta < 0$; solve $\theta/(1 + \theta^2) = -0.45$ and keep the invertible root
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question}: an ARMA(2,1) leaves $Q^*(10) = 15.2$ in its residuals. Reject at 5\%?
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{Answer}: degrees of freedom $10 - 3 = 7$, $\chi^2_{0.95}(7) = 14.07 < 15.2$: reject; with 10 degrees of freedom (critical 18.31) one would wrongly accept
    \end{itemize}
    \item Next: \tsachlink{https://danpele.github.io/Time-Series-Analysis/EN/Courses/chapter3_unit_roots_arima_models.pdf}{Chapter 3}, unit roots and ARIMA models: what to do when a root sits on the unit circle
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
